_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Iraq covering Mesopotamia (cradle of civilisation), Sumer, Akkad, Babylon, Assyria, Achaemenid/Seleucid/Parthian/Sassanid rule, Islamic conquest and Abbasid Caliphate (Baghdad golden age), Mongol sack of Baghdad 1258, Ottoman Iraq, British Mandate, Hashemite monarchy, 1958 revolution, Ba'ath Party, Saddam Hussein, Iran-Iraq War, Gulf War 1991, sanctions, US invasion 2003, sectarian civil war, ISIS, and post-ISIS reconstruction.

religion.note: Shia majority but Sunni minority historically ruled (Ottoman/Ba'ath); Yezidi genocide by ISIS 2014; Iraqi Christians (Chaldean, Assyrian, Syriac) declined from 1.5M to ~200,000

ethnic_groups.name: Arab
ethnic_groups.notes: Both Shia (southern/central) and Sunni (western/northern); tribal society remains important; Iraqi Arabic dialect

ethnic_groups.name: Kurdish
ethnic_groups.notes: Northern Iraq (Kurdistan Region); Sorani and Kurmanji dialects; KRG autonomous since 1991; peshmerga; Anfal genocide under Saddam; Halabja chemical attack 1988

ethnic_groups.name: Turkmen
ethnic_groups.notes: Kirkuk, Tal Afar, Mosul; Turkic; both Sunni and Shia; contested Kirkuk; third-largest group

ethnic_groups.name: Assyrian/Chaldean/Syriac
ethnic_groups.notes: Indigenous Christians; Aramaic-speaking; Nineveh Plains; massive emigration due to violence; Chaldean Catholic Church largest denomination

ethnic_groups.name: Yezidi
ethnic_groups.notes: Sinjar/Shekhan; Kurdish-speaking; Yezidi syncretic religion; ISIS genocide August 2014; Nadia Murad Nobel Prize 2018

ethnic_groups.name: Mandaean (Sabian)
ethnic_groups.notes: Gnostic; Mandaic (Aramaic); baptismal religion; southern marshlands; mostly emigrated (50,000 to ~5,000)

ethnic_groups.name: Shabak
ethnic_groups.notes: Nineveh; mixed Turkic-Kurdish-Arab heritage; Shia majority; distinct syncretic beliefs; targeted by ISIS

ethnic_groups.name: Marsh Arab (Ma'dan)
ethnic_groups.notes: Southern marshlands; reed house culture; Saddam drained marshes 1991; partially restored; unique wetland civilisation; UNESCO heritage

ethnic_groups.name: Other (Feyli Kurd, Black Iraqi, Circassian, Armenian)
ethnic_groups.notes: Feyli Kurds (Shia Kurds, deported by Saddam); small Black Iraqi community (Basra, slave trade heritage); Armenian remnant

current_leader.name: Mohammed Shia' Al Sudani
current_leader.title: Prime Minister
current_leader.notes: Coordination Framework (Shia coalition); backed by pro-Iran factions; relatively technocratic; infrastructure focus

president.name: Abdul Latif Rashid
president.title: President (ceremonial, Kurdish by convention)
president.notes: PUK; Kurdish; convention reserves presidency for Kurds, PM for Shia, speaker for Sunni

former_leaders.name: King Faisal I
former_leaders.notes: Hashemite; installed by British; first king; Arab Revolt veteran; unified Iraq's communities

former_leaders.name: King Faisal II
former_leaders.notes: Last king; killed in 14 July Revolution 1958 (military coup by Qasim)

former_leaders.name: Abdul Karim Qasim
former_leaders.notes: Brigadier; overthrew monarchy; left Baghdad Pact; killed in 1963 Ba'athist coup

former_leaders.name: Saddam Hussein
former_leaders.notes: Ba'ath Party; Tikrit; invaded Iran (1980-1988); gassed Halabja; invaded Kuwait 1990; Gulf War; sanctions; toppled by US invasion March 2003; captured December 2003; executed December 2006

former_leaders.name: Nouri al-Maliki
former_leaders.notes: Da'wa Party; Shia; sectarian policies contributed to ISIS rise; US troop withdrawal 2011

former_leaders.name: Haider al-Abadi
former_leaders.notes: Da'wa; led war against ISIS; Mosul liberation 2017

910.name: Sumerian Civilization and the Dawn of History
910.description: The cradle of civilization in Mesopotamia — the invention of writing, the first cities, the Sumerian city-states, and the empires of Akkad and Ur III.

sub_clusters.name: Ubaid and Uruk Periods
sub_clusters.description: The earliest urban settlements in southern Mesopotamia, the Ubaid culture, the Uruk expansion, and the invention of cuneiform writing — humanity's first writing system.
key_events: Uruk becomes the world's first major city (c. 3500 BC)
Invention of cuneiform writing in southern Mesopotamia (c. 3400–3100 BC)

sub_clusters.name: Early Dynastic Period and Akkadian Empire
sub_clusters.description: The Sumerian city-states of Ur, Lagash, and Uruk, the Epic of Gilgamesh, and Sargon of Akkad's creation of the world's first empire.
key_events: Sargon of Akkad unifies Mesopotamia — first known empire in history (c. 2334 BC)
Composition of the Epic of Gilgamesh, the oldest great literary work

sub_clusters.name: Third Dynasty of Ur
sub_clusters.description: The Sumerian renaissance under the Third Dynasty of Ur (Ur III), Ur-Nammu's law code — predating Hammurabi — the Great Ziggurat of Ur, and the eventual collapse under Amorite and Elamite pressure.

910.name: Babylonian and Assyrian Empires
910.description: The great empires of Mesopotamia — Old Babylon under Hammurabi, the Neo-Assyrian military superpower, and the Neo-Babylonian splendor of Nebuchadnezzar II.

sub_clusters.name: Old Babylonian Kingdom and Hammurabi
sub_clusters.description: The rise of Babylon under the Amorite dynasty, Hammurabi's famous law code, the unification of Mesopotamia, and the Hittite sack of Babylon.
key_events: Hammurabi issues his famous law code — one of the oldest deciphered legal documents (c. 1754 BC)

sub_clusters.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
sub_clusters.description: The Neo-Assyrian Empire as the ancient world's greatest military power, its vast extent from Egypt to Iran, Ashurbanipal's Library of Nineveh, and the dramatic fall of the empire.
key_events: Ashurbanipal creates the Library of Nineveh — first systematically organized library (c. 650 BC)
Fall of Nineveh to the Medes and Babylonians (612 BC)

sub_clusters.name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
sub_clusters.description: Nebuchadnezzar II's magnificent rebuilding of Babylon, the Hanging Gardens, the Ishtar Gate, the Babylonian Captivity of the Jews, and the Persian conquest by Cyrus the Great.
key_events: Nebuchadnezzar II destroys Jerusalem and deports Jews to Babylon (586 BC)
Cyrus the Great conquers Babylon (539 BC)

910.name: Persian, Hellenistic, and Parthian Mesopotamia
910.description: Mesopotamia under successive foreign empires — Achaemenid Persia, Alexander's conquest, the Seleucid cities, and the Parthian capital at Ctesiphon.

sub_clusters.name: Achaemenid and Seleucid Mesopotamia
sub_clusters.description: Mesopotamia as a wealthy satrapy of the Persian Empire, Alexander's conquest and death in Babylon, the founding of Seleucia on the Tigris, and Greek cultural influence.

sub_clusters.name: Parthian Mesopotamia and Ctesiphon
sub_clusters.description: The Parthian capture of Mesopotamia, the establishment of Ctesiphon as the winter capital, the Roman-Parthian wars, and the trading kingdom of Hatra.

920.name: Sassanid Mesopotamia and Arab Conquest
920.description: Mesopotamia as the heartland of the Sassanid Empire, the grand capital of Ctesiphon, the founding of the garrison cities of Basra and Kufa, and the Arab Muslim conquest.

sub_clusters.name: Sassanid Iraq
sub_clusters.description: The Sassanid Arch of Ctesiphon (Taq Kasra), the Lakhmid Arab client kingdom at al-Hira, the Nestorian Christian community, and the Jewish academies of Babylonia producing the Talmud.

sub_clusters.name: Arab Conquest and Garrison Cities
sub_clusters.description: The Battle of al-Qadisiyyah, the founding of Basra and Kufa as military camps that became major cities, the assassination of Ali at Kufa, and Iraq's centrality to the Sunni-Shia split.
key_events: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah — Arab forces defeat the Sassanid army (636 AD)
Assassination of Caliph Ali at Kufa — foundational event of the Sunni-Shia schism (661 AD)

920.name: Abbasid Caliphate and Baghdad's Golden Age
920.description: The Abbasid revolution and the founding of Baghdad, the Islamic Golden Age of science and learning, and the city's status as the cultural capital of the world.

sub_clusters.name: Founding of Baghdad and Early Abbasids
sub_clusters.description: The Abbasid overthrow of the Umayyads, Caliph al-Mansur's founding of Baghdad as the 'Round City,' Harun al-Rashid's legendary court, and the Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom).
key_events: Caliph al-Mansur founds Baghdad as the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate (762 AD)
The House of Wisdom translates Greek, Persian, and Indian works into Arabic (c. 830 AD)

sub_clusters.name: Abbasid Decline and Buyid-Seljuk Control
sub_clusters.description: The Samarra period, the weakening of caliphal authority, Buyid Shia and Seljuk Sunni domination of the caliphs, and the twilight of Abbasid Baghdad before the Mongol catastrophe.

930.name: Mongol Destruction and Ilkhanid Iraq
930.description: The catastrophic Mongol sack of Baghdad ending the Abbasid Caliphate, the destruction of the irrigation system, and Iraq's transformation from the center of civilization to a provincial backwater.

sub_clusters.name: Fall of Baghdad (1258)
sub_clusters.description: Hulagu Khan's siege and sack of Baghdad, the execution of Caliph al-Musta'sim, the destruction of the Grand Library, and the end of the Islamic Golden Age.
key_events: Hulagu Khan sacks Baghdad — estimated hundreds of thousands killed (1258)
Last Abbasid Caliph al-Musta'sim executed, ending 508 years of the caliphate (1258)

sub_clusters.name: Jalairid and Timurid Devastation
sub_clusters.description: The Jalairid Sultanate's rule from Baghdad, Timur's devastating sack of Baghdad in 1401, and the irreversible destruction of Iraq's ancient irrigation infrastructure.

930.name: Ottoman Iraq
930.description: The Ottoman conquest of Iraq, the division into the vilayets of Mosul, Baghdad, and Basra, the Safavid-Ottoman wars, and the Mamluk governors of Baghdad.

sub_clusters.name: Ottoman Conquest and Safavid Rivalry
sub_clusters.description: Suleiman the Magnificent's conquest of Baghdad, repeated Safavid reconquests, and the Treaty of Zuhab finally establishing Ottoman control over Mesopotamia.
key_events: Suleiman the Magnificent captures Baghdad from the Safavids (1534)
Treaty of Zuhab permanently divides Iraq and Iran between Ottoman and Safavid spheres (1639)

sub_clusters.name: Mamluk Governors of Baghdad
sub_clusters.description: The Georgian Mamluk dynasty governing Baghdad with near-autonomy from Istanbul, the plague and flood that devastated Baghdad in 1831, and the reimposition of direct Ottoman control.

940.name: Late Ottoman Iraq and Tanzimat
940.description: The reimposition of direct Ottoman rule, Midhat Pasha's modernizing reforms, the first oil explorations, and the strategic interests of Britain, Germany, and the Ottoman Empire.

sub_clusters.name: Tanzimat Reforms in Iraq
sub_clusters.description: Midhat Pasha's modernizing governorship introducing land reform, schools, hospitals, newspapers, and steamship navigation on the Tigris — transforming Iraq's economy and society.

sub_clusters.name: European Competition and Oil
sub_clusters.description: The Berlin-Baghdad Railway concession, British strategic concerns about the Persian Gulf, early oil exploration, and the creation of the Turkish Petroleum Company.
key_events: Turkish Petroleum Company formed to explore Iraqi oil (1912)

940.name: British Mandate and Hashemite Kingdom
940.description: The British conquest during WWI, the League of Nations mandate, the installation of King Faisal I, the 1920 revolt, oil concessions, and the road to independence and revolution.

sub_clusters.name: WWI Conquest and 1920 Revolt
sub_clusters.description: The British Mesopotamian campaign, the disastrous Siege of Kut, the 1920 Iraqi revolt against British rule — one of the largest uprisings in the Middle East — and the Cairo Conference.
key_events: Great Iraqi Revolt against British rule — over 6,000 British and 8,000 Iraqi casualties (1920)
Faisal I installed as King of Iraq at the Cairo Conference (1921)

sub_clusters.name: Hashemite Monarchy and Oil Economy
sub_clusters.description: The Hashemite kingdom under British influence, the 1925 Mosul Question, the Iraq Petroleum Company's exploitation of Kirkuk oil, the 1941 Anglo-Iraqi War, and growing nationalist sentiment.

950.name: Republican Iraq and Baathist Rule
950.description: The 1958 revolution, the rise of the Ba'ath Party, Saddam Hussein's dictatorship, the Iran-Iraq War, the invasion of Kuwait, and international sanctions.

sub_clusters.name: 1958 Revolution and Early Republic
sub_clusters.description: The Qasim-led revolution overthrowing the monarchy, the volatile early republic, Qasim's overthrow, the first Ba'athist coup, and the Arif brothers' rule.
key_events: 14 July Revolution — overthrow and killing of King Faisal II and the royal family (1958)

sub_clusters.name: Saddam Hussein Era
sub_clusters.description: Saddam Hussein's consolidation of power, the Iran-Iraq War, the Anfal genocide against the Kurds, and the invasion and annexation of Kuwait leading to the Gulf War.
key_events: Anfal campaign — genocide against Iraqi Kurds using chemical weapons (1986–1989)
Iraq invades Kuwait; US-led coalition liberates Kuwait in the Gulf War (1990–1991)

sub_clusters.name: Sanctions and No-Fly Zones
sub_clusters.description: Crippling UN sanctions devastating Iraq's civilian population, the Kurdish autonomous region in the north, the Shia uprising suppression, and the UN Oil-for-Food program.

960.name: US Invasion, Civil War, and Reconstruction
960.description: The 2003 US-led invasion, the fall of Saddam, the sectarian civil war, the rise and defeat of ISIS, and Iraq's ongoing struggle for stability and sovereignty.

sub_clusters.name: 2003 Invasion and Occupation
sub_clusters.description: The US-led invasion based on disputed WMD intelligence, the fall of Baghdad, the dissolution of the Iraqi army, de-Ba'athification, and the descent into insurgency and sectarian violence.
key_events: US-led coalition invades Iraq; Saddam's regime falls within weeks (March–April 2003)
Bombing of the al-Askari Shrine triggers full-scale sectarian civil war (February 2006)

sub_clusters.name: Sectarian Civil War and US Surge
sub_clusters.description: The devastating Sunni-Shia civil war, the Anbar Awakening, the US troop surge, and the gradual reduction in violence leading to the US military withdrawal.

sub_clusters.name: Rise and Defeat of ISIS
sub_clusters.description: The Islamic State's blitzkrieg capturing Mosul and declaring a caliphate, the horrific persecution of Yazidis and minorities, and the Iraqi-led military campaign to liberate all territories.
key_events: ISIS captures Mosul and declares a caliphate (June 2014)
Iraqi forces liberate Mosul after nine months of brutal urban warfare (July 2017)

sub_clusters.name: Post-ISIS Iraq and Tishreen Protests
sub_clusters.description: The October 2019 Tishreen protest movement demanding an end to corruption and Iranian influence, the government crackdown, political instability, and reconstruction challenges.

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
